title: Venlafaxine: Serotonin, Norepinephrine, and Blood Pressure
bottomLine: Venlafaxine is an SNRI used for depressive and anxiety disorders. Monitor mood and suicidality, blood pressure, serotonin toxicity, sodium risk in susceptible patients, and discontinuation symptoms if therapy is reduced too quickly.
recognize: Common effects include nausea, insomnia or somnolence, sweating, sexual dysfunction, and possible blood-pressure elevation.
Serotonin syndrome risk rises when combined with other serotonergic agents.
priorities: Assess mood, suicidal thoughts, blood pressure, medication adherence, and interacting serotonergic drugs.
Escalate new suicidality, severe hypertension, serotonin-syndrome findings, seizure, or marked discontinuation symptoms.
assessMonitor: Trend mood, BP, sleep, sodium risk when clinically indicated, and adverse effects after dose changes.
interventions: Administer consistently and reinforce gradual tapering when discontinuation is ordered.
medicationSafety: Do not stop abruptly unless an emergency requires it; withdrawal symptoms can be significant.
Avoid combining with MAO inhibitors and review other serotonergic agents.
teaching: Improvement may take time; report worsening mood, severe agitation, or unusual neurologic symptoms promptly.
delegationScope: Routine medication administration may be within PN scope depending on setting; suicide-risk assessment and acute mental-status changes require licensed-nurse escalation.
examTrap: Stopping venlafaxine suddenly because the patient feels better.
oneLinePearl: With venlafaxine, watch mood, pressure, serotonin, and the taper.

title: Duloxetine: Mood, Neuropathic Pain, and Liver Safety
bottomLine: Duloxetine is an SNRI used for depression/anxiety and several chronic pain conditions. Monitor mood, blood pressure, liver-risk context, serotonin toxicity, urinary retention, falls, and discontinuation symptoms.
recognize: Nausea, dry mouth, somnolence, constipation, and dizziness are common.
Heavy alcohol use or significant chronic liver disease increases concern for hepatic injury.
priorities: Review liver history, alcohol use, BP, urinary symptoms, fall risk, and serotonergic interactions.
Escalate jaundice, dark urine, severe abdominal pain, serotonin-syndrome findings, or suicidality.
assessMonitor: Trend mood, BP, liver-related symptoms, pain response, urinary retention, and orthostasis/falls.
interventions: Administer delayed-release product intact unless product instructions specify otherwise; taper when discontinuing.
medicationSafety: Avoid unsafe combinations with MAO inhibitors and other serotonergic agents.
Abrupt discontinuation can cause withdrawal symptoms.
teaching: Report liver symptoms, new suicidal thinking, and severe dizziness; do not stop suddenly without a plan.
delegationScope: Medication administration and reinforcement of teaching may be within PN scope; worsening depression or acute toxicity requires escalation.
examTrap: Treating duloxetine as only an antidepressant and ignoring liver/alcohol history or urinary retention.
oneLinePearl: Duloxetine treats mood and pain—but the liver, BP, and serotonin still matter.

title: Mirtazapine: Sedation, Appetite, and Mood Monitoring
bottomLine: Mirtazapine is an antidepressant often associated with sedation and increased appetite/weight. Monitor mood and suicidality, daytime sedation/falls, weight/metabolic change, and rare but important neutropenia or serotonin toxicity.
recognize: Somnolence, increased appetite, weight gain, and dry mouth are common.
Fever, sore throat, or infection symptoms can be concerning if severe neutropenia occurs.
priorities: Assess suicide risk, sedation, fall risk, weight/appetite changes, and infection symptoms.
Escalate severe infection signs, suicidal intent, or serotonin-syndrome findings.
assessMonitor: Trend mood, sleep, weight, fall risk, and CBC if clinically indicated by infection symptoms or orders.
interventions: Schedule consistently; bedtime administration is common when sedation is desired and prescribed.
medicationSafety: Additive sedation occurs with alcohol, opioids, benzodiazepines, and other CNS depressants.
redFlags: High fever with severe sore throat
teaching: Use caution with driving until effects are known; report fever/sore throat and worsening mood promptly.
delegationScope: Routine administration may be within PN scope; acute suicide risk and severe adverse effects require escalation.
examTrap: Assuming sedation and appetite increase mean the drug is automatically ideal for every older adult.
oneLinePearl: Mirtazapine can help sleep and appetite—while increasing fall and weight risk.

title: Trazodone: Sedation, Orthostasis, and Priapism
bottomLine: Trazodone is an antidepressant with prominent sedating and alpha-blocking effects. Watch for orthostatic hypotension/falls, serotonin toxicity, QT-related risk in susceptible patients, and priapism, which is an emergency.
recognize: Drowsiness and dizziness are common.
A prolonged painful erection requires urgent medical treatment to prevent permanent injury.
priorities: Assess fall risk, BP/orthostasis, interacting sedatives/serotonergic drugs, and cardiac-risk context.
Escalate priapism, syncope, serious arrhythmia symptoms, serotonin syndrome, or suicidality.
assessMonitor: Trend mood, sleep, BP, falls, cardiac symptoms, and serotonergic adverse effects.
interventions: Use fall precautions when sedation/orthostasis is significant.
medicationSafety: Additive sedation occurs with alcohol and other CNS depressants.
teaching: Rise slowly and report a prolonged erection, fainting, or worsening mood immediately.
delegationScope: Routine administration may be within PN scope; emergent adverse effects require immediate escalation.
examTrap: Treating trazodone as a harmless sleep aid and missing orthostasis or priapism.
oneLinePearl: Trazodone can sedate and drop pressure; priapism is the cannot-miss emergency.

title: Methylphenidate: Stimulant Benefit With Abuse and Cardiac Risk
bottomLine: Methylphenidate is a CNS stimulant used for ADHD and selected sleep disorders. Current labeling carries a boxed warning for abuse, misuse, and addiction; also monitor BP/HR, appetite/weight, growth in children, sleep, and new psychotic/manic symptoms.
recognize: Decreased appetite, insomnia, abdominal discomfort, and increased pulse/BP can occur.
Misuse risk is clinically important because methylphenidate is a Schedule II controlled substance.
priorities: Assess cardiac history, BP/HR, appetite/weight, sleep, misuse/diversion risk, and mental-status changes.
Escalate chest pain, syncope, severe hypertension, psychosis, mania, or suicidal behavior.
assessMonitor: Trend BP/HR, weight, pediatric growth, sleep, symptom control, and misuse behaviors.
interventions: Administer product-specific formulation correctly; many extended-release products must not be crushed.
medicationSafety: Secure controlled medication and watch for diversion.
MAOI interactions can be dangerous; medication reconciliation matters.
teaching: Do not share stimulant medication; store securely and follow the exact formulation instructions.
delegationScope: Controlled-substance administration and counting follow facility/state rules; adverse-effect assessment requires licensed clinical judgment.
examTrap: Focusing only on attention improvement while ignoring weight loss, BP rise, or misuse risk.
oneLinePearl: Stimulants improve focus—but appetite, pressure, sleep, and misuse are part of the prescription.

title: Atomoxetine: Nonstimulant ADHD With Suicidality Monitoring
bottomLine: Atomoxetine is a nonstimulant norepinephrine-reuptake inhibitor for ADHD. Current U.S. labeling carries a boxed warning for suicidal thoughts/behaviors in pediatric patients; monitor BP/HR, mood/behavior, liver symptoms, urinary retention, and rare priapism.
recognize: Appetite decrease, GI symptoms, fatigue, and BP/HR increases can occur.
New suicidal thinking or major behavior change is a high-priority cue in children/adolescents.
priorities: Assess mood/suicide risk, BP/HR, liver symptoms, urinary symptoms, and cardiac history.
Escalate suicidal intent, jaundice, severe cardiovascular symptoms, or priapism.
assessMonitor: Trend behavior/mood, BP/HR, growth/weight in pediatric patients, and liver-related symptoms.
interventions: Administer consistently and reinforce that therapeutic effect is not immediate.
medicationSafety: Use caution with drugs that strongly inhibit CYP2D6 or raise BP/HR.
teaching: Families should report abrupt behavior changes or suicidal thoughts promptly; do not expect stimulant-like immediate effects.
delegationScope: Routine administration may be within PN scope; suicide-risk assessment and serious toxicity require escalation.
examTrap: Assuming nonstimulant means no cardiovascular or suicide-monitoring concerns.

title: Buprenorphine/Naloxone: Treat OUD Without Triggering Withdrawal
bottomLine: Buprenorphine/naloxone combines a partial opioid agonist with an antagonist component and is used for opioid use disorder. Safe induction requires appropriate withdrawal timing; monitor sedation/respiratory status, CNS-depressant interactions, adherence/diversion, and overdose risk from relapse or attempts to override opioid blockade.
recognize: Starting too soon after full-agonist opioid exposure can precipitate withdrawal.
Benzodiazepines, alcohol, and other sedatives increase respiratory-depression risk.
priorities: Confirm the treatment plan, recent opioid exposure/withdrawal status, sedation level, respiratory status, and interacting CNS depressants.
Escalate severe precipitated withdrawal, respiratory depression, overdose, or diversion concerns.
assessMonitor: Trend withdrawal/craving, sedation, respiratory rate, adherence, oral health, and concurrent sedative use.
interventions: Administer sublingual/buccal product exactly as directed and do not swallow prematurely.
Support naloxone availability and comprehensive OUD treatment.
medicationSafety: Do not abruptly discontinue without a plan because relapse/withdrawal risk can rise.
Current labeling recommends considering access to an opioid-overdose reversal agent.
teaching: Avoid alcohol/nonprescribed sedatives; store securely; know how/when to use naloxone; maintain follow-up.
delegationScope: Controlled-substance administration and OUD-program responsibilities vary by setting/state; acute respiratory or withdrawal assessment requires licensed-nurse escalation.
examTrap: Giving buprenorphine/naloxone immediately after full-agonist opioid use without considering precipitated withdrawal.
oneLinePearl: Buprenorphine helps OUD—but induction timing and respiratory safety matter.

title: Extended-Release Naltrexone: Opioid-Free First
bottomLine: Extended-release naltrexone is an opioid antagonist used for alcohol dependence and prevention of relapse to opioid dependence after detoxification. The patient must be opioid-free before initiation to avoid severe precipitated withdrawal, and overdose risk can rise when blockade wanes or after treatment stops.
recognize: Trying to override opioid blockade with large opioid doses can cause fatal overdose.
Injection-site reactions and hepatic injury are important adverse effects.
priorities: Verify opioid-free status and absence of acute withdrawal or current opioid analgesic use.
Assess liver symptoms, injection site, mood, and overdose-risk education.
Escalate precipitated withdrawal, severe injection-site injury, or opioid overdose.
assessMonitor: Trend abstinence/relapse risk, liver-related symptoms, mood, injection site, and opioid exposure.
interventions: Use only the approved deep IM gluteal administration process when authorized and trained.
medicationSafety: Current labeling recommends an opioid-free interval before initiation.
Loss of opioid tolerance increases overdose vulnerability after missed doses/discontinuation.
teaching: Carry overdose-reversal access when recommended and tell all clinicians that opioid blockade is present before pain treatment.
delegationScope: IM administration and substance-use treatment responsibilities vary by state/facility; adverse-event assessment requires escalation.
examTrap: Giving extended-release naltrexone to a patient who is still physiologically opioid-dependent.
oneLinePearl: Naltrexone starts after opioids are out—not while dependence is active.

title: Acamprosate: Maintain Alcohol Abstinence, Check the Kidneys
bottomLine: Acamprosate supports maintenance of alcohol abstinence after the patient is already abstinent. It is renally cleared, so renal function is central to safe use; diarrhea is common and severe renal impairment is a contraindication.
recognize: Acamprosate does not treat acute alcohol withdrawal or intoxication.
Mood changes and suicidality should still be monitored in recovery care.
priorities: Confirm abstinence-focused treatment plan and renal function.
Assess diarrhea, hydration, adherence, mood, and relapse risk.
Escalate suicidal intent or severe renal dysfunction concerns.
assessMonitor: Trend renal function as ordered, GI tolerance, adherence, mood, and recovery supports.
interventions: Administer delayed-release tablets intact and pair medication with psychosocial support.
medicationSafety: Dose reduction is required in moderate renal impairment and severe renal impairment is contraindicated per current label.
teaching: This medication supports abstinence; it does not make drinking physically impossible and does not treat withdrawal.
delegationScope: Routine administration may be within PN scope; suicide-risk or relapse-withdrawal complications require escalation.
examTrap: Using acamprosate to treat acute alcohol withdrawal.
oneLinePearl: Acamprosate is for staying abstinent, not detox—and kidneys decide safety.

title: Disulfiram: Alcohol Exposure Can Become an Emergency
bottomLine: Disulfiram inhibits aldehyde metabolism so alcohol exposure can produce flushing, vomiting, hypotension, tachycardia, chest symptoms, and severe reactions. It works only when the patient understands and accepts abstinence; monitor liver toxicity and hidden alcohol sources.
recognize: Alcohol may be present in mouthwashes, sauces, cough products, aftershaves, or other products depending on formulation.
Hepatotoxicity can occur even without prior liver disease.
priorities: Confirm informed participation, recent alcohol abstinence, liver-risk context, and interacting products/medications.
Escalate severe disulfiram-alcohol reaction, hypotension, chest pain, dyspnea, or hepatic-injury symptoms.
assessMonitor: Trend liver-related symptoms/labs as ordered, adherence, alcohol exposure, mood, and recovery supports.
interventions: Reinforce avoidance of all ethanol-containing products and use as part of a comprehensive recovery plan.
medicationSafety: Never give disulfiram to an intoxicated patient or without the patient's knowledge.
Review metronidazole and other clinically important interactions.
teaching: Avoid alcohol in beverages and products; reactions can occur after medication has been stopped because enzyme inhibition persists.
delegationScope: Medication administration may be within PN scope when ordered; severe reaction or hepatic symptoms require immediate escalation.
examTrap: Administering disulfiram as a coercive consequence to a patient who has not consented to abstinence treatment.
oneLinePearl: Disulfiram turns alcohol exposure into toxicity—consent and avoidance are the safety plan.
